Read more: https://aws.amazon.com/bedrock/faqs/

prompt:
A chat assistant on Amazon Bedrock sends the whole conversation history with every request so the model can follow the thread. The team notices that each turn costs more than the one before it, even though users type short messages.

What explains the rising cost?

options.text: Bedrock bills chat sessions by the minute once they pass a threshold
options.explanation: On-demand text models are billed per input and output token; there is no per-minute session charge.

options.text: Every request re-sends earlier turns, so input tokens grow each turn
The price per output token rises as a conversation gets longer
options.explanation: The per-token rate is fixed for a model and tier; what grows is the number of tokens sent.

options.text: The model raises its temperature as the history grows
options.explanation: Temperature is set by the caller and does not change by itself; it also has no effect on price.

explanation: Models are stateless, so a chat app re-sends prior turns as input tokens on every call. Each new turn adds to that history, so input tokens, and the cost per request, climb steadily. Trimming or summarizing history, or caching a fixed prefix, keeps this in check. Rates per token stay the same and there is no session-time charge. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/count-tokens.html

prompt:
A support agent holds long conversations. After many turns, the history approaches the model's context window and the agent starts losing facts the customer gave early on. The team wants to keep those facts while staying under the token limit.

Which approach should the team take?

options.text: Raise the maximum output tokens setting for each response
options.explanation: Maximum output tokens caps the length of the reply; it does nothing to fit a growing input history into the context window.

options.text: Fine-tune the model on transcripts of past support conversations
options.explanation: Fine-tuning teaches general patterns from old data; it cannot hold the facts of the current customer's live conversation.

options.text: Drop the oldest turns once the history reaches a fixed length
options.explanation: A plain sliding window stays under the limit but discards the early facts the team wants to keep.

options.text: Summarize older turns and keep the most recent turns verbatim

explanation: Context engineering decides what goes into the limited context window. Summarizing older turns keeps their key facts in a few tokens while recent turns stay word for word; Strands Agents ships a summarizing conversation manager for this. A sliding window loses early facts, output token limits do not shrink the input, and fine-tuning cannot store a live conversation. Read more: https://strandsagents.com/latest/documentation/docs/user-guide/concepts/agents/conversation-management/

prompt:
A team is improving the quality of an assistant's answers by changing what goes into the model's context window for each request, without changing the model.

Which TWO are context engineering practices? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Add only the most relevant retrieved chunks instead of whole documents
Switch the model to Provisioned Throughput to remove throttling
options.explanation: Provisioned Throughput changes capacity and billing; it does not change what information the model sees.

options.text: Store user preferences in long-term memory and inject the relevant ones
Raise the temperature so the model explores more possible answers
options.explanation: Temperature changes how tokens are sampled from the same context; it adds no information to the context.

options.text: Move to a model with more parameters trained on more data
options.explanation: Changing the model is model selection; the team is working on what goes into the context, with the model fixed.

explanation: Context engineering is the practice of choosing and shaping everything a model sees for a request: instructions, retrieved passages, memory, tool results and history. Retrieving only relevant chunks and injecting relevant stored preferences, for example from AgentCore long-term memory, give the model better information within the token budget. Capacity, sampling settings and model size do not change the context. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/memory.html

prompt:
A travel agent built by one team needs to delegate hotel bookings to a separate booking agent that another team builds and runs as its own service. The two agents must exchange tasks and results.

Which protocol is designed for this communication?

options.text: Agent2Agent (A2A)
Model Context Protocol (MCP)
options.explanation: MCP standardizes how an agent connects to tools and data sources; communication between independent agents is what A2A was designed for.

options.text: OpenAPI schema in a Bedrock action group
options.explanation: An action group describes APIs or Lambda functions one agent can call as tools; it is not a protocol for peer agents to exchange tasks.

options.text: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway
options.explanation: Gateway turns APIs and Lambda functions into MCP tools for an agent; it is not the protocol two peer agents use to exchange tasks.

explanation: Agent2Agent (A2A) is an open protocol that lets agents built by different teams or frameworks discover each other and exchange tasks and results across services. MCP connects an agent to tools and data; an OpenAPI action group gives a Bedrock agent callable APIs; AgentCore Gateway exposes tools over MCP. AgentCore Runtime and Strands Agents both support A2A. Read more: https://strandsagents.com/latest/documentation/docs/user-guide/concepts/multi-agent/multi-agent-patterns/

prompt:
A company built one Amazon Bedrock agent for billing, technical support and returns. It has 40 tools and long instructions, and it often calls the wrong tool for a request.

Which design change most directly addresses this?

options.text: Give the agent a model with a larger context window
options.explanation: A larger window fits the instructions but leaves one agent choosing among all 40 tools, which is what causes the errors.

options.text: A supervisor agent that routes each request to specialist agents
Fine-tune the model on examples from the three areas
options.explanation: Fine-tuning is costly and slow to change, and one agent still sees every tool for every request.

options.text: Put the documentation for the three areas in a knowledge base
options.explanation: A knowledge base adds retrieval of documents; it does not reduce the number of tools the agent has to choose from.

explanation: Amazon Bedrock multi-agent collaboration lets a supervisor agent pass each request to collaborator agents, each with a narrow role, its own instructions and a small set of tools. Smaller toolsets make tool choice more reliable and each specialist easier to test. A bigger context window, fine-tuning or a knowledge base all leave one agent juggling every tool. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents-multi-agent-collaboration.html

prompt:
An airline's booking agent runs on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. When a customer returns weeks later in a new session, the agent should remember that the customer prefers aisle seats.

Which capability meets this requirement?

options.text: AgentCore Memory short-term memory
options.explanation: Short-term memory keeps turn-by-turn context within a single session, so the preference is gone when a new session starts weeks later.

options.text: A model with a larger context window
options.explanation: A context window holds what is sent in the current request; it keeps nothing between sessions.

options.text: AgentCore Memory long-term memory
Prompt caching on the agent's instructions
options.explanation: Prompt caching reuses a repeated prompt prefix for a few minutes to save cost; it does not store facts about a user.

explanation: AgentCore long-term memory extracts key facts such as user preferences from conversations and keeps them across sessions, so the agent can offer an aisle seat next time. Short-term memory covers one session, a context window covers one request, and prompt caching only reuses identical prefixes briefly. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/memory.html

prompt:
A deployed writing assistant lets users rate each draft. After three months the team has thousands of ratings, many low ones on legal topics.

What is the best use of this data in the FM lifecycle?

options.text: Archive it for compliance and keep the current model unchanged
options.explanation: Keeping the data for audit is fine, but ignoring it skips the feedback stage that drives the next improvement.

options.text: Pre-train a new foundation model from scratch on the ratings
options.explanation: A few thousand ratings are far too little for pre-training, which needs very large unlabeled datasets and heavy compute.

options.text: Switch to the largest available model without further testing
options.explanation: A bigger model may or may not fix legal drafts, and deploying without evaluation skips a lifecycle step.

options.text: Use it to refine prompts or tuning data, re-evaluate, then redeploy

explanation: Feedback closes the FM lifecycle loop: production signals show where the model falls short, the team improves prompts, retrieval or fine-tuning data for those cases, evaluates again and redeploys. Ignoring the signal stalls improvement, ratings are not pre-training material, and swapping models without evaluation skips a step. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/generative-ai-lens/generative-ai-lifecycle.html

prompt:
An internal assistant answers questions about company tax rules. Several rules changed after the foundation model was trained, and the assistant quotes the old rates. The rules change several times a year.

Which approach fixes this with the least ongoing effort?

options.text: Lower the temperature so answers stay close to what the model knows
options.explanation: Lower temperature makes output more consistent, but the model still knows only the old rates.

options.text: Fine-tune the model on the new rules each time they change
options.explanation: Fine-tuning can add the new rules, but retraining several times a year costs far more effort than updating documents.

options.text: Retrieve the current rules from company documents and add them to the prompt
Move to a larger foundation model from the same provider
options.explanation: A larger model has its own training cutoff and still lacks company rules published after it.

explanation: The problem is a knowledge cutoff: the model only knows its training data. Retrieval augmented generation (RAG) pulls the current rules into each prompt, so an update is just a document change. Lower temperature and a bigger model do not add new facts, and repeated fine-tuning is costly for facts that change often. Read more: https://aws.amazon.com/what-is/retrieval-augmented-generation/

prompt:
A legal team wants each 300-page contract summarized in a single request. A contract is about 180,000 tokens. Two models score the same on the team's quality tests: Model A has a 32,000-token context window and is cheaper per token; Model B has a 300,000-token context window.

Which model should the team choose?

options.text: Model A, because its lower price per token matters most at scale
options.explanation: Price only matters among models that can do the job, and a 180,000-token contract does not fit in a 32,000-token window.

options.text: Model B, because the whole contract fits in its context window
Model A, with the maximum output tokens set high enough for the contract
options.explanation: Maximum output tokens limits the reply length; it does not raise the input context window.

options.text: Model B, because larger context windows give more accurate summaries
options.explanation: The two models scored the same on quality; the deciding factor is that only Model B can take the whole input.

explanation: Model choice starts with hard constraints. A single-request summary of a 180,000-token contract needs a context window larger than that, so only Model B qualifies; cost per token is then irrelevant. Output token limits do not change input capacity, and a larger window is not in itself a sign of better quality. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/models-supported.html

prompt:
A company wants one foundation model to draft content for its legal, marketing and engineering departments. Leadership asks whether a candidate model performs well across all three.

Which evaluation answers that question?

options.text: Score the model on a public general-knowledge benchmark
options.explanation: A general benchmark gives one overall number and says little about this company's three specific kinds of content.

options.text: Score it on test prompts from each department and compare per department
Measure the average latency of its responses under load
options.explanation: Latency is a performance requirement, but it says nothing about whether the content is good in each department.

options.text: Count the tokens it produces per request for each department
options.explanation: Token counts reflect length and cost, not whether the drafts are accurate or useful.

explanation: Cross-domain performance means checking quality in each domain the model will serve. A test set with prompts from each department, scored separately (for example with an Amazon Bedrock model evaluation job), shows whether the model holds up everywhere or is weak in one area. A general benchmark, latency or token counts do not answer that. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/evaluation.html

prompt:
A team has built an agent with the open-source LangGraph framework. They want to run it in production with each user session isolated from the others, fast scaling, and no servers to manage, while keeping their LangGraph code.

Which option fits best?

options.text: Amazon SageMaker JumpStart

prompt:
An agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore must read each user's calendar in a third-party SaaS app on that user's behalf. Users grant consent through OAuth, and the team wants no credentials stored in the agent's code.

AgentCore Memory

prompt:
A customer-facing app on Amazon Bedrock needs the fastest possible responses during busy business hours. Traffic is low at night, so the company wants to avoid paying for reserved capacity around the clock, and it accepts a higher per-token price for these requests.

Which option fits best?

options.text: The Reserved tier with a one-month term
options.explanation: The Reserved tier bills for reserved tokens-per-minute capacity for the whole term, which the company wants to avoid.

options.text: The Flex tier
options.explanation: Flex trades longer processing times for a discount, the opposite of the fastest responses.

options.text: The Priority tier
Batch inference with results written to Amazon S3
options.explanation: Batch jobs return results asynchronously in S3, which cannot serve users waiting in the app.

The Reserved tier bills for capacity around the clock, Flex is slower and cheaper, and batch inference is asynchronous. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/service-tiers-inference.html

prompt:
A data science team fine-tuned an open-weight Llama model in Amazon SageMaker AI. They want to call the resulting model through the same serverless Amazon Bedrock API their applications use for other models, with no endpoint to manage.

Which feature should they use?

options.text: Amazon Bedrock Custom Model Import
Amazon Bedrock Marketplace
options.explanation: Bedrock Marketplace offers models from providers to deploy on endpoints; it is not how you bring weights you trained yourself.

options.text: Amazon Bedrock Model Distillation
options.explanation: Distillation trains a smaller student model from a teacher's responses; it does not bring in a model trained elsewhere.

options.text: Amazon SageMaker JumpStart
options.explanation: JumpStart deploys models to SageMaker AI endpoints the team manages, which the team wants to avoid.

Marketplace lists provider models, Distillation creates a new student model, and JumpStart leaves the team running an endpoint. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-customization-import-model.html

prompt:
A help-desk assistant on Amazon Bedrock uses a large model for every request. About 70% of questions are simple and a smaller model in the same family answers them just as well; the rest need the large model. Questions arrive in any order, and the team wants to cut cost with little engineering effort and no quality loss on hard questions.

Which option meets these requirements?

options.text: Switch the assistant to the smaller model in the same family
options.explanation: This cuts cost but lowers quality on the 30% of hard questions, which breaks a stated requirement.

options.text: Enable prompt caching for the assistant's requests
options.explanation: Caching saves cost on a repeated prompt prefix, but these short, varied questions share little that could be cached.

options.text: Provisioned Throughput for the large model
options.explanation: Reserved capacity still runs every simple question on the large model, and hourly billing suits steady, high traffic.

options.text: Intelligent prompt routing in the same model family

explanation: Intelligent prompt routing gives one serverless endpoint that predicts, per request, which model in a family will answer well, and sends simple prompts to the cheaper model and hard ones to the larger model. That cuts cost without building a classifier. Moving everything to the small model hurts hard questions, caching needs a repeated prefix, and Provisioned Throughput does not change which model answers. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prompt-routing.html

prompt:
A large model in Amazon Bedrock gives the quality a company needs for classifying insurance claims, but at the planned volume its cost and latency are too high. A smaller model in the same family is fast and cheap but less accurate on this task. The company has thousands of real claim prompts but no reviewed answers for them.

Which approach best meets the goal?

options.text: Supervised fine-tuning of the smaller model on the claim prompts
options.explanation: Supervised fine-tuning needs labeled prompt-and-response pairs, and the company has prompts without reviewed answers.

options.text: Model distillation with the large model as teacher
Provisioned Throughput for the large model
options.explanation: Reserved capacity can steady latency under load, but every request still runs on the expensive large model.

options.text: Continued pre-training of the smaller model on the prompts
options.explanation: Continued pre-training adapts a model to a domain's language from large unlabeled text; it does not transfer the large model's task skill.

explanation: Amazon Bedrock Model Distillation takes prompts, has the larger teacher model generate responses, and fine-tunes the smaller student model on them. The student gains task accuracy close to the teacher at the student's lower cost and latency, and no human-labeled answers are needed. Supervised fine-tuning needs labeled pairs, Provisioned Throughput keeps the expensive model, and continued pre-training targets domain language rather than the task. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-distillation.html

prompt:
A report generator on Amazon Bedrock sends about 500 input tokens per request and receives about 4,000 output tokens. For the chosen model, an output token costs four times as much as an input token. The team wants the biggest cost reduction.

Which change should the team make?

options.text: Enable prompt caching on the 500-token prompt
options.explanation: Caching discounts repeated input tokens, and input is only about 500 of the 16,500 cost units per request here.

options.text: Shorten the report instructions to save 200 input tokens
options.explanation: Saving 200 input tokens trims little, because output tokens make up most of the cost.

options.text: Ask for a tighter report and cap the maximum output tokens
Send requests through a cross-Region inference profile
options.explanation: Cross-Region inference raises throughput and availability; it does not reduce how many tokens are billed.

explanation: Cost is input tokens times the input price plus output tokens times the output price. Here input is 500 units and output is 4,000 x 4 = 16,000 units, so output drives about 97% of the cost. Asking for a tighter report and capping output tokens attacks that share; caching or trimming the short prompt saves little, and cross-Region routing does not change the token bill. Read more: https://aws.amazon.com/bedrock/pricing/

prompt:
A company is choosing a model in Amazon Bedrock for a claims app. Requirements: accept a photo and a text description in one request; process data in an EU Region; respond within 2 seconds at the 95th percentile; and, among models that qualify, cost the least. The candidates:

- Model A: text only, available in the EU, 1 s, lowest cost
- Model B: image and text, available in the EU, 1.5 s, medium cost
- Model C: image and text, available in US Regions only, 1 s, low cost
- Model D: image and text, available in the EU, 4 s, low cost

Which model should the company choose?

options.text: Model A
options.explanation: Model A is fast, cheap and in the EU, but it cannot accept the photo, so it fails the first requirement.

options.text: Model B
Model C
options.explanation: Model C is fast and multimodal, but processing in US Regions breaks the EU data requirement.

options.text: Model D
options.explanation: Model D is multimodal, in the EU and cheaper than B, but its 4-second response time misses the 2-second target.
